So the Śūraṅgama Sūtra teaches two kinds of dharma: “Principle belongs to sudden awakening, and with the awakening all is dissolved; phenomena must be removed gradually, and are exhausted by stages.” As soon as the principle is explained, one awakens at once; after awakening, all habits dissolve, one wants nothing, and at once all is empty and pure. Such people certainly exist, but they are only a few, an extremely small number — people of the very highest faculties, returners. If one is not a returner, one cannot, upon a single awakening, be thoroughly clear. Yet today’s suddenness is the gradualness of former days. It has been accumulated through practice in the past, and the past, and further past, slowly, slowly, and so today it drops off at a single “crack.” The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says, “Principle belongs to sudden awakening, and with the awakening all is dissolved; phenomena must be removed gradually, and are exhausted by stages.” This originally teaches two dharma-gates: one the perfect and sudden dharma, one the gradual dharma. The very few of the highest faculties, returners, hear the principle and awaken at once, and all habits are destroyed in the instant of awakening, so that spiritual powers and wondrous function can appear. Most people of middling and lower faculties must, after awakening, train amid affairs and gradually remove their habits before they can slowly bring their function into play. Now we may as well join the two dharma-gates into one: “principle belongs to sudden awakening, phenomena must be removed gradually” — cultivating the sudden and the gradual gates together. Why say this? Because we are now in the age of the Dharma’s decline, when beings’ faculties are dull and their obstacles heavy, and they cannot awaken suddenly, cultivate suddenly, and realize suddenly; so we must join the two gates into one, protecting and sustaining after awakening the principle, diligently removing habits, and gradually developing penetration and realizing the fruit. To join sudden awakening and gradual cultivation and speak of them together does not hold together logically, but it accords with the present actual situation and so may be borrowed. This principle is not easy to explain clearly; we may as well use a story from the time when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world to illustrate. Two disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha were discussing a sentence the Buddha had spoken; each had his own reasons, and neither would yield, so they went to ask the Buddha: Buddha, which of us speaks in accord with your meaning? The Buddha said: neither of you accords with my meaning, but both of your meanings can be used. Why? Because they accord with the actual situation! So now we can only speak of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.

Then how does one cultivate? Pure Land people recite the Buddha-name: “Amitābha, Amitābha” — using this Buddha-name to sweep clean the defilement in our minds, sweep clean the habits in our minds, sweep clean our afflictions. The moment affliction emerges, recite “Amitābha” aloud and turn the mind to emptiness, dissolve it into emptiness. And Chan people? They attend to the huatou at every moment. The moment affliction stirs, ask: “Who are you?” — a blow straight to the head: “Who stirred this affliction? Who is it that stirs affliction?” A blow straight to the head — this is attending to the huatou. Tantric practitioners, the moment affliction arises, immediately recite a mantra to transform it. The methods differ, but the principle is the same. Do not say: my Pure Land is good and your Chan is wrong; my Chan is good and your Pure Land is wrong; my tantra is good and your Chan and Pure Land are both wrong. That is dividing into sects and households, and shows that you have not yet understood. When you understand and bring forth wondrous function, you will say: Chan is good, Pure Land is good, tantra is good — all are means; the expedient gates are many, but the return to the source is one road. Borrowing the power of the Buddha-dharma, we apply effort in practice, sweep clean our habits, and dissolve our afflictions into emptiness, and so “when the ice melts the water flows and moistens, and only then does the work of irrigation appear; when delusion is exhausted the mind is empty and penetrating, and the function of penetrating radiance responds and appears.” When the mind-flower is penetrating and bright, spiritual powers are revealed and wondrous function is boundless. All this is realized by practice; if you say there is no need to cultivate, will that do? It will not! So one must cultivate.
Someone asks: for one who has awakened, when the end of life comes, where does the spirit-nature go?

This is a great question! After awakening to the Way, where does one go? Many people ask this. A man from Hong Kong wrote to ask me whether one who has awakened should know in advance, at the end of life, where he is going — that is, foreknow the place. If he does not foreknow the place, then he has not awakened. Is this right? No! Why not? If one has truly awakened, there is no birth and no death, no coming and no going — what place is there? As I said just now, this wondrous existence true mind is subtle form, and subtle form is space; what place does space have? If you want a place, then there is still coming and going, still birth and death, and you have not yet awakened. The writer did not understand this principle, and so asked where one goes when the span of life ends and one dies. This is not only his question but everyone’s question. So today, borrowing a passage from Chan Master Guifeng, let us speak of this again. Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi said:

All beings are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment — numinous, luminous, empty, and still — no different from the Buddha. But because from beginningless kalpas they have never understood or awakened, they falsely cling to the body as the mark of self, and so give rise to love and hate and other emotions. Following emotion they create karma, and following karma they receive retribution. Birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth. Yet the nature of enlightenment within the body has never been born or died: like one driven about in a dream while the body itself lies at ease; like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature, it is the dharma-body, originally unborn — what reliance would it have? Numinously undimmed, vividly ever aware, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet through many lives of false clinging, habit has become nature, and joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly. Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these emotions are hard to remove at once. One must constantly be aware, reducing and again reducing, like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside. How could the cultivation of one lifetime equal the powers and functions of all the Buddhas? One need only take empty stillness as one’s own essence and not acknowledge the form-body; take numinous knowing as one’s own mind and not acknowledge deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them. Then at the end of life karma naturally cannot bind one. Though there is an intermediate state, one goes where one will, and may lodge at will among the heavens or among humans. If the thoughts of love and hate are already extinguished, one does not receive a body of segment-by-segment birth and death, and can of oneself change the short into the long, the coarse into the subtle. If the subtle flowing is utterly stilled and extinguished, and only the great perfect wisdom of enlightenment shines alone, then one responds to capacities and manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation-bodies to deliver beings with affinity — this is called a Buddha.
Now let me explain this passage of Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi:

All beings are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment — numinous, luminous, empty, and still — no different from the Buddha.” All beings — not only we humans, but ants, insects, flies, lions, apes, and so on — are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment. Which being would you say lacks the nature of enlightenment? Look at a mosquito: if you have blood here, it flies over at once to bite you. A fly: set out a piece of steamed cake, and it can fly from far away to land on it. They have the nature of enlightenment. Of humans there is no need to speak. The nature of enlightenment is the nature of knowing and awareness: do you know that your belly is hungry? Do you know that the weather is warm today? These are all the nature of knowing and awareness! So all beings possess the nature of enlightenment. “Numinous, luminous, empty, and still” means numinous yet luminous, radiant and transparent, vividly clear. It is radiance, and its numinous knowing is vivid and unmoving, thus, thus. This “luminous” has two explanations: “empty” — utterly nothing, with not one thing established; “still” — unmoving and unshaking, neither coming nor going. “No different from the Buddha” means no distinction whatsoever, no second difference, from Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Maitreya Buddha, and all other Buddhas.

But because from beginningless kalpas they have never understood or awakened, they falsely cling to the body as the mark of self, and so give rise to love and hate and other emotions.” “Beginningless” means having no beginning, and in the future no end either, going round and round, always like this. “Never understood or awakened” means never having awakened, never having known that one is oneself a great treasure. The Lotus Sūtra uses the analogy: a man has a maṇi jewel sewn into his clothing and does not know it. This maṇi jewel can rain down all treasures, and so you are not poor. You are complete in everything; whatever you want, it has. Yet you do not know it, and go begging outside. Just as our present revolving in the six paths and wandering in birth and death is begging. We have a great treasure and do not know it; we have never understood or awakened. “Falsely cling to the body as the mark of self”: through false clinging one does not recognize the true but takes the false as real. This body is fundamentally not “I,” yet it is taken as “I.” The body is like the house we live in, and within it there is a person. What is the person? The person is our numinous luminous true mind. Not knowing this, one takes the “house” as “I”: this body is me, this body is me! “And so give rise to love and hate and other emotions.” Thus love and hate and other emotions arise. I like this and dislike that; this person is friendly to me and that person is unfriendly. There is much discrimination, all of it deluded thought. What one likes one takes as one’s own; what one dislikes one strikes down — and so one creates karma and receives retribution.

Following emotion they create karma, and following karma they receive retribution. Birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth.” Birth and death fundamentally do not exist; they arise because, after we have love and hate and other emotions, we create karma according to the mind. We want something and cannot get it, and it belongs to another, so we rob him or kill him — this creates the karma of killing. Creating karma means receiving retribution and revolving in the six paths. Creating good karma one ascends to the heavens; creating evil karma one falls into the hells; birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth. Alas! There was fundamentally no birth and death, yet we have fallen into birth and death. Appearing and disappearing in the six paths, born and dying again and again, without liberation.

Yet the nature of enlightenment within the body has never been born or died: like one driven about in a dream while the body itself lies at ease; like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change.” Though we revolve in birth and death again and again within the six paths, our nature of enlightenment has never been born or died; it is not born because you are born, nor extinguished because your flesh dies. If you fall into hell it is not pained; if you ascend to heaven it is not glad. It is originally neither born nor extinguished, empty, numinous, and abiding nowhere, never having been born or died, never having moved. It is like being in a dream, chased by villains, terrified beyond measure, running madly on, while in fact the body still lies peacefully in bed, unmoving. It is also like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change. This is an analogy for the fact that although we revolve in the six paths, the Buddha-nature does not change.

If one can awaken to this nature, it is the dharma-body, originally unborn — what reliance would it have?” If we can awaken to this nature of enlightenment as the dharma-body and understand that our nature of enlightenment is the root of all things and matters, that it was originally never born and never extinguished, why should it still have a place to rely on? If you have truly awakened, you should have no reliance and no place to go. I remember a man from Wenzhou who said something very funny. He claimed to have awakened, and someone asked him: “We are not people who practice the Pure Land method seeking birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; we practice the Chan school — after we pass away, where do we go?” See how he answered: he said, “One may lean on grass and attach to trees, or on a rock, or on a great tree, or on withered grass — anywhere will do.” Oh no, that is bad — he has become a spirit clinging to grass and trees! How can that do? To lean on grass and attach to trees is to be a ghost clinging to a body. In Shanghai’s Fuxing Park there is a thousand-year-old bodhi tree said to be inconceivably efficacious, and everyone goes to worship it; in fact it is a ghost, a spirit-ghost attached to it. After death, to lean on grass and attach to trees is to become a ghost — what kind of Way would you say he has awakened to? In fact it has nothing to do with the Way; it is all false. Our nature of enlightenment is “originally unborn — what reliance would it have?” There should be no reliance. One who leans on grass and attaches to trees has never caught a glimpse of even half a thread of the nature of enlightenment.

Long ago there was a broken stove abandoned for many years, and a spirit attached itself to the stove and sent people a dream: come and make offerings to me on this stove, and whatever you want I will give you. Everyone said, there is a spirit on this stove, let us all go and make offerings! Many people came to make offerings to him, and the spirit satisfied their wishes. Word spread from one to ten and from ten to a hundred, and this broken stove became extraordinarily famous. There was a Chan master in that region (a disciple of National Master Hui’an), who saw that this spirit attached to the broken stove was causing everyone to kill living beings to make offerings to him and so create karma, and so he went and taught it the Dharma. Striking the stove with his staff — thump, thump, thump — he said: I ask you, you are compounded of bricks, tiles, and mud; where does the spirit come from? Where does the god come from? Bricks, tiles, and mud have no spirit and no god; the consciousness that has spirit is your own mind — why do you attach yourself to this stove of brick and mud? At a single pointer from the Chan master the stove spirit awakened: right, the spirit is not on the bricks, tiles, and mud — the spirit is in my own mind! He hurriedly abandoned the broken stove. That night he came to thank the Chan master and then ascended to heaven. Afterwards everyone called this Chan master “the Monk Who Abandoned the Broken Stove,” and his real name was forgotten. Even Chan knows not to cling to the body; can we manage it while clinging to grasses and trees? So there must be no reliance! We are originally unborn, originally without reliance!

Numinously undimmed, vividly ever aware, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.” If you have truly awakened to the Way, you are vividly ever aware and numinously undimmed, and everywhere is you. Wherever there is affinity, there you manifest a body. Hence it is called “the nirvāṇa of no abode.” There is no fixed place; you can manifest a body anywhere, and wherever there is affinity you can manifest. If one has truly and thoroughly awakened, how could there still be a fixed place? To have a fixed place is to be unawakened. “Numinously undimmed” means not the slightest mark of dimness. “Vividly ever aware” means utterly clear and bright. This knowing has no interruption, and so it is called ever aware. It is not that one knows now and after a while does not know — that would be useless. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere: if it does not come, how can it go? If there is coming there is going, and if there is going there is coming; all are relative, and all that is relative is false. It is the absolute true mind, and so it has no coming or going, no entering or emerging.

blocks.text: 9. Knowing One’s Own Mind as It Really Is

inline.s: Next we are shown how to apply effort and realize the Way, and thereby become Buddhas.

Yet through many lives of false clinging, habit has become nature, and joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly.” What we are now explaining is the supreme-vehicle Chan: “One’s own mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is one’s own mind.” That you can hear this dharma and believe it without doubt means that your good roots were not planted with one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas, but were planted over many lives and kalpas.

But through many lives and kalpas we have grown used to false clinging; we cling to outer states as real, cling to the body as “I,” and habit has become second nature. Oh, this body is me, most precious, do not touch me! In fact it is a stinking night-soil bucket — what is there to prize? A Qing dynasty emperor fell in love with a concubine whose body had a fragrance; this Fragrant Concubine was from Xinjiang and was said to have a rare fragrance about her. What fragrance was it? The stench of fox! Yet the old emperor called it fragrance. It is clear that whether anything is beautiful or not has no fixed standard: what you like is good, and otherwise it is hateful. Or having grown used to it, what is not good is also not bad. As the saying goes: stay long in a shop of salted fish and you no longer smell the stench. Once a habit is formed it is hard to turn back. This is an unshakable truth. Hearing this, someone may think: “This body is me. And everyone thinks so; you say the body is not me — who will believe you?” Alas! Through many lives and kalpas we have falsely clung to outer states, grown used to it, and made it a habit. Thus we have produced all kinds of views about states and things, judging and measuring everything by our own likes and dislikes: what suits my mind I grasp, and otherwise I reject. Hence “joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly.” Joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, fear, alarm, and grief — everyone has them. When things accord with my mind I am all smiles; when they offend my mind I am furious; when I lose something I am sullen; when something pleases me I beam. These are all the subtle flowing.

The subtle flowing is extremely subtle deluded thought moving without cease. The most fundamental deluded mind consists of the five omnipresent mental factors: intention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition. These five omnipresent dharmas are in fact a single thought arising in the mind, good or evil; they exist within the eight consciousnesses and constantly stir up all the good and evil seeds in the eight consciousnesses. They are extremely, extremely subtle, and so are called the arising and ceasing of the flowing. What is called flowing is like a ceaseless stream of water — but this water is not like the towering waves of the great ocean, nor the rolling billows of rivers, but like a small brook flowing softly, faintly, and finely. In fact it flows extremely fast, so fast that it does not show its movement; ordinarily you cannot see it and think it is unmoving — this is subtle, extremely subtle deluded thought. We spoke earlier of coarse delusion, which is deluded thought arising when facing circumstances. If you know that circumstances are your mind and your mind is circumstances, then you do not cling. Without clinging, coarse deluded thoughts do not arise. But the subtle deluded seeds are still there. They are subtle and extremely subtle; you see them as if unmoving, yet in fact they move very fast. How can the subtle flowing be cut off? Only by entering deeply into the samādhi of Vajrasattva can one see it and destroy it; without the samādhi of Vajrasattva it is useless. So one must enter deep samādhi. One who recites the Buddha-name must attain the samādhi of Buddha-recitation; without it, it will not do. One who practices Chan must raise a great mass of doubt; once the great doubt is raised, deluded thoughts do not move and the mass of doubt envelops the whole body, and when the time and conditions arrive, with a “crack” it bursts open, and only then can one personally see the nature. Tantric practitioners are the same: with the blessing of the three mysteries of body, mouth, and mind, borrowing the Buddha’s power to empower us and push us forward, until conditions ripen and — crack! — it explodes and cuts off the subtle flowing! This subtle flowing is extremely subtle; you cannot see it, and only by doing the work and settling down can you see it. For example, in a cup of turbid water you cannot see the silt within; once it settles and the water above is clear, you see how much silt there is below. While it is stirred and turbid, you cannot see it. You must first settle, and only then can you see the subtle flowing.

Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these emotions are hard to remove at once.” We say the mind is Buddha and the Buddha is the mind. This is the truth; you awaken to it at once: yes, yes! We are originally Buddhas — if not Buddhas, how could we speak? Could we still ask who is reciting the Buddha-name? If not Buddhas, how could we recite the Buddha-name? If not Buddhas, how could we write? If not Buddhas, how could we walk? When this body’s breath stops it does not move; movement is the wondrous function of the Buddha-nature. The truth is suddenly awakened to and understood, but “these emotions are hard to remove at once.” Emotion is deluded emotion, the emotion of love. The emotion of love is hard to remove! The ancients said: “If reciting the Buddha-name were like thinking of love, we would long ago have realized the Way!” If reciting the Buddha-name were like thinking of love, we would long ago have realized the Way.

We ordinary beings find it hard to give up the emotion of love, and the scope of love is very broad: the love of men and women, of mother and child, of husband and wife, the love of music, beauty, dogs, and horses, and many other attachments, such as fondness for antiques, stamp collecting, calligraphy and painting, growing flowers, keeping birds, and so on. There are truly far too many things people love. For a woman the hardest to cut off is the love of mother and child: once she has a child it is forever in her heart and can never be forgotten, and even at death she cannot let go: I cannot bear to leave my child! There was an old woman who recited the Buddha-name; at the end of her life we urged her: “Let go, and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.” She said: “I am not going; I cannot bear to leave my children and grandchildren!” With such delusion, how could she be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Ordinary beings all find “these emotions hard to remove at once.” “At once” means immediately. Our emotions are very hard to remove immediately, and so we can only awaken suddenly and cultivate gradually. Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation is a matter of necessity, yet it suits the habits of beings in this Sahā world at the present stage. Do not sing lofty tunes and say that you are one of sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, and sudden realization, needing no cultivation, no cultivation no attainment no realization. It is very easy to say with the mouth, but can you truly do it? Boasting is useless; you must truly do it. If you boast, King Yama will not let you off; he will still send you an invitation. Only if you truly do it can King Yama’s invitation be cancelled.

One must constantly be aware, reducing and again reducing, like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside.” One must be aware for a long time — this is doing the work. For example, one who practices the Pure Land school simply raises the Buddha-name: the moment a thought stirs, quickly raise the Buddha-name high and recite it aloud: “Amitābha, Amitābha, Amitābha...” and so dissolve the deluded emotion. If the deluded emotion is not dissolved, it will not do! “Reducing and again reducing” means reducing the deluded emotion day by day, reducing your habits, afflictions, and clinging day by day — reducing, reducing, and reducing still further. Deluded emotion cannot be removed in a single day: “like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside.” As soon as the wind blows, waves arise, and after the wind stops the waves still surge, and only slowly do they come to rest. So the ancients said: “The wind stops but the waves still surge; principle appears but thoughts still invade.” “Principle appears” — the truth appears and one awakens; yet “thoughts still invade,” deluded thoughts still intrude, and so one must remove them slowly.

How could the cultivation of one lifetime equal the powers and functions of all the Buddhas?” To cultivate for a single lifetime and expect at once to have the three insights and six superknowledges of all the Buddhas, and the same powers as all the Buddhas — that cannot be done. Though we have not yet developed the three insights and six superknowledges, we must believe deeply and without doubt: our mind is the Buddha-mind, and apart from this there is no Buddha-mind.

Speaking of this, I want to discuss an important question with everyone. I have heard people say: the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is not awakening; only when both subject and object are forgotten is there awakening. In fact they do not understand what the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is, do not recognize the original, and yet pretend to be of great faculties; they have not read the books of the teachings, yet they chatter irresponsibly.

Long ago, when Dharma Master Chengguan was expounding the Avataṃsaka Sūtra to Empress Wu Zetian (do not think Empress Wu Zetian was bad! Empress Wu Zetian was an awakened emperor. The present sūtra-opening verse, “The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma, in a hundred thousand million kalpas hard to encounter; now that I see and hear it and can receive and uphold it, may I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning,” was composed by Wu Zetian in praise of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and is now used as the sūtra-opening verse for all scriptures), he said to her: “When not a single thought arises and the preceding and following intervals are cut off, the illuminating substance shines brightly — this is the thus, thus Buddha.” When not a single thought arises, the preceding and following intervals are cut off. The preceding interval is the preceding thought; the following interval is the following thought. The preceding and following intervals are cut off with a “crack.” The illuminating substance is the essence that can illumine all things and bring forth all wondrous function — the nature. “Brightly” means not clinging to any mark. “The thus, thus Buddha” — this is the Buddha! See how clearly he put it. Yet some do not understand and say that the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is not awakening. They do not know what the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is, and still pretend to be good teachers — are they not harming people! Not knowing themselves yet deluding others, they will fall into hell as swiftly as an arrow flies!
